moved.sentence: **Cross-cutting concerns are noted, not isolated.** When a concern appears across all scope groups, note it in findings as cross-cutting and move on.

judged.note: should-note-cross-cutting-concerns-not-isolate keeps noting an all-groups concern as cross-cutting in findings and moving on, plus 'noted, not isolated', at SHOULD.

moved.sentence: Do not create a scope group whose members are "all the places that call log()".

judged.note: should-not-group-call-sites keeps the prohibition on a scope group of 'all the places that call log()', at SHOULD NOT.

moved.sentence: **Shared infrastructure gets exactly one scope group.** If a concern has its own files (a Logger class, a SessionManager), those files form one scope group.

judged.note: should-give-shared-infrastructure-one-scope-group keeps that a concern's own files (Logger class, SessionManager) form exactly one scope group.

moved.sentence: **Logging infrastructure vs logging call sites.** The `OSLog` / `Logger` configuration file is infrastructure.

judged.note: should-classify-logging-configuration-as-infrastructure keeps the OSLog/Logger configuration file as infrastructure, and the rationale repeats the sentence verbatim.

moved.sentence: **Pervasive coupling is an architectural smell, not a decomposition strategy.** If every scope group directly calls a `GlobalSingleton`, note the anti-pattern — the solution is to inject the dependency, not to merge all groups into one because they share the dependency.

judged.note: The two rules keep noting the GlobalSingleton anti-pattern, the 'smell, not a decomposition strategy' claim, and inject-not-merge as the remedy.

moved.sentence: **Security/auth infrastructure is always its own scope group.** Never treat auth enforcement as merely cross-cutting — the SessionManager and token lifecycle have real behavior and state and warrant their own scope group (separate from where auth checks are enforced).

judged.note: The MUST rule keeps auth infrastructure as always its own group, separate from enforcement points, and the MUST NOT keeps 'never merely cross-cutting'; the rationale keeps the real-behavior-and-state reason.
